query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
final_answer: Across the studies, sustainability reporting is generally presented as a way to make sustainability performance visible, accountable, and comparable, often by using established frameworks such as GRI and related ESG standards [https://openalex.org/W4402984150||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers also link sustainability reporting directly to the SDGs: one says GRI-based reporting is a powerful tool for showing whether SDGs matter to the private sector and how firms contribute to them, while another provides a roadmap for reporting using the SDG Compass logic model [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4297090192||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence from supply chain-focused papers suggests this link is not just firm-level but also chain-level, because sustainable supply chain practices are positively associated with both SDGs and financial performance, and sustainability assessment frameworks can measure both a company’s and suppliers’ sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. The supply chain perspective also matters because green supply chain research connects sustainability into sourcing, resilience, circular economy, and digital transformation, with SDGs 9, 12, and 17 appearing especially connected in the bibliometric mapping [https://openalex.org/W4388635591||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, sustainability performance is repeatedly tied to better outcomes when sustainability is integrated into operations and strategy, including improved financial performance, operational efficiency, and reduced environmental and social impacts [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4394855216||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the evidence is not uniformly positive: one study reports no correlation in reporting specific SDGs and a disconnection between corporate sustainability performance and SDG reporting, suggesting that firms may report SDGs without grounding them in actual performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study notes that some categories have no direct or indirect SDG connection because of limited life-cycle thinking in the SDGs and weak discussion for stakeholders such as workers, consumers, and value chain actors [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the literature suggests sustainability reporting, SDGs, and sustainability performance are linked most strongly when reporting is embedded in supply chain, life-cycle, or ESG assessment frameworks rather than treated as a separate disclosure exercise [https://openalex.org/W4404433455||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, which multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared, and what did the sensitivity analysis reveal about their suitability and differences in calculation and interpretation?
final_answer: The clearest district-heating-specific comparison in the supplied evidence is a study that evaluated five MCDA methods: WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, across 8 criteria and 12 district heating companies [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Its sensitivity analysis varied criterion weights in three ways to test stability of alternative rankings and average scores, including a comparison of AHP-derived weights with equal weights [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The study concluded that all five methods were suitable for sustainability analysis of district heating systems, but that they differ in calculation process and in how results are interpreted [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. In the broader district-heating literature, MCDM is described as the preferred evaluation framework, and AHP is reported as the most frequently used method, although those summaries do not provide a direct multi-method comparison or sensitivity results [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. A related sustainability assessment study in energy system transformation pathways compared WSM, PROMETHEE II, and TOPSIS and found that top ranks were not completely stable across methods, but that some scenario clusters were consistently high, medium, or low across all methods [https://openalex.org/W4200438885||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that multiple MCDA approaches can be applied to sustainability assessment, but that sensitivity to weighting and ranking differences means no single method fully dominates in all cases [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4200438885||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the sustainability ideas in the supply chain management framework and the article on sustainable marketing both show how environmental sustainability can be advanced and linked to company image?
final_answer: Across the supply chain management papers, environmental sustainability is advanced by treating it as a systems-level, cross-functional, and cross-stakeholder practice rather than a stand-alone initiative [https://openalex.org/W3211582089||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3183301120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308101885||ABSTRACT||000]. These studies consistently emphasize collaboration, coordination, stakeholder engagement, supplier relationships, and organizational learning as mechanisms that embed sustainability into supply chains and improve decisions and production/consumption patterns [https://openalex.org/W3211582089||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3183301120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308101885||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers also frame sustainability as broader than environmental protection alone, tying it to social and economic concerns through triple-bottom-line or socioecological approaches [https://openalex.org/W3211582089||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283697438||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4224002953||ABSTRACT||000]. In terms of company image, the clearest evidence is indirect: one paper says there is a gap between what companies say about sustainability and what they actually do, so a credible sustainability mindset matters because declarations alone are not enough [https://openalex.org/W4364359925||ABSTRACT||000]. Other studies similarly suggest that sustainability supports a positive business identity by linking it to sustainable business models, value creation, and improved firm performance, including financial performance and corporate environmental management [https://openalex.org/W3175142938||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283697438||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000]. One framework also notes that sustainability efforts can produce unintended negative outcomes, showing that implementation is not automatically beneficial [https://openalex.org/W4224002953||ABSTRACT||000]. Because no evidence chunk for the sustainable marketing article was provided, the answer can only synthesize how the supply chain literature links sustainability to company image, not directly compare both articles [https://openalex.org/W4364359925||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3183301120||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enablers of Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises because they improve environmental performance, resource efficiency, and sustainable operations [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000]. In particular, clean energy, green manufacturing, green logistics, and reverse logistics are described as creating conditions for industry development and future growth by supporting Industry 4.0 technologies and innovations in the SDG context [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also links Industry 4.0 to SDG-aligned sustainability through circular economy practices and the ReSOLVE framework, especially for SDGs 6, 7, 9, 12, and 13 [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000]. Several reviews find that these technologies can reduce waste, improve traceability and resource management, and lower environmental impact across production and supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, one review warns that Industry 4.0 and related technologies can also harm sustainability through air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive raw material, information, and energy consumption if implemented poorly [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Evidence on enterprise adoption is strongest in the Slovak enterprise study, where more than 82% of surveyed enterprises reported implementing the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001]. That study also found significant relationships between environmental management in the context of SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics, including waste separation and recycling, environmental certification, employee environmental training, renewable energy use, and continuous CO2 reduction in logistics activities [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001]. Broader reviews similarly conclude that widespread Industry 4.0 adoption has enhanced sustainability performance and helped address environmental concerns while supporting innovation and policy decisions, including in the UAE context [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence base is still uneven: warehouse-focused research says sustainable Industry 4.0 is at an early stage with only a few articles and major barriers such as weak government support, legal issues, lack of skilled manpower, political issues, and old warehouses, especially in developing countries [https://openalex.org/W4288738282||ABSTRACT||001].

final_answer: The systematic review on OSC describes its environmental performance as positive, stating that OSC has enhanced outcomes in environmental issues such as waste generation and carbon emissions [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, it emphasizes that market adoption was still limited by 2018, because no major market had exceeded 20% OSC penetration [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000]. The review treats it as timely to identify the factors that advanced and enhanced OSC’s environmental performance because it seeks to draw lessons from current research and compare developments in developed and developing countries [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000]. In particular, the goal is to understand differences, similarities, critical success factors, and future opportunities across these regions [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000]. Other provided reviews do not add direct evidence on OSC’s 2018 market penetration or this timing rationale, although they do reinforce that sustainability and environmental performance remain important research themes [https://openalex.org/W4385812085||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4401931324||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests a field where environmental benefits are recognized, diffusion is still relatively low, and cross-regional comparison is needed to explain how stronger environmental performance emerged [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the study use predictive analytics in the 1-hop work, and what does the 2-hop AI impact assessment say about AI"s role for sustainable development?
final_answer: Across the 1-hop studies, predictive analytics is used as part of AI-driven monitoring, forecasting, and optimization to improve sustainability outcomes. For example, one paper describes “advanced predictive models and monitoring systems” for better resource monitoring, climate-change mitigation, and biodiversity promotion, while another links predictive analytics with cleaner production to optimize resources, reduce carbon footprint, and eliminate waste across industries [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000]. A further study says AI supports real-time data analysis, predictive modeling, and optimization in environmental science, including environmental monitoring, climate-change prediction, conservation, biodiversity, and sustainable resource management [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the literature on SDG-related research shows deep learning and supervised machine learning are prominent for forecasting and system optimization, although only a few studies combine advanced AI applications with deep sustainability expertise [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000]. The 2-hop impact assessments are consistent in portraying AI as broadly beneficial for sustainable development, with significant potential across environmental, economic, and social dimensions [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers specify that AI can help achieve sustainability goals through lower energy and material use, better waste handling, better resource efficiency, and support for SDGs or net-zero-related goals [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4405499395||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence repeatedly notes that AI’s benefits are conditional on supportive policies, infrastructure, regulation, data quality, and explainability, and that high costs, privacy concerns, technical skill needs, and social resistance can limit impact [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401830906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000]. Expert and review-based assessments are also optimistic: one Delphi study reports an overall positive role for AI in sustainable development with especially positive impacts for SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15, while Goals 16 and 17 are neutral [https://openalex.org/W4396674183||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that AI is being used as a forecasting and optimization tool in the 1-hop work and is seen in the 2-hop assessments as a central enabler of sustainable development, but one whose real-world value depends on governance, infrastructure, and interdisciplinary implementation [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
final_answer: Across the EU literature, the SDGs are consistently presented as a framework for policy coherence because they connect environmental, social, and economic objectives into a single sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers argue that coherence is achieved by aligning EU policy instruments and governance layers, including the Green Deal, European Semester CSRs, recovery planning, and national priorities, so that policies reinforce rather than undermine one another [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that this coherence is uneven in practice: environmental goals are described as the most complex and least coherent SDGs in the EU, with biodiversity and climate needing stronger monitoring and data [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also emphasizes that policy coherence requires attention to territorial diversity, because EU-wide monitoring should be localized and customized to capture different regional progress and challenges [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000]. Tool-based approaches such as Life Cycle Assessment, circular economy analysis, and regional indicator sets are presented as ways to support coherence by improving policy design, monitoring, and comparability across contexts [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000]. However, one paper warns that the SDG framing can create an apolitical façade: technical and “win-win” solutions may obscure genuinely political incoherencies and limit transformative change [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the EU research landscape is said to have poor intra-cluster connections and a need for more transdisciplinary and system-level research that explicitly addresses trade-offs and context-specific priorities [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that SDGs are used as a coordinating reference for sustainable development policy in the EU, but they differ on whether current institutional and analytical arrangements are sufficient to deliver truly transformative coherence [https://openalex.org/W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402759895||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.notes: The cited chunks explicitly say the SDGs provide a framework for tracking multiple dimensions of sustainability and that policy coherence across environmental, social, and economic goals is a key challenge.

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
final_answer: Across the provided studies, the three themes connect through a common message: sustainability in the built environment depends not only on environmental benefits but also on overcoming implementation barriers in practice [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000]. The off-site construction review presents environmental sustainability as a core advantage of OSC, especially through improved waste generation and carbon-emission performance, yet it also notes that no major market exceeded 20% OSC penetration by 2018, showing a gap between promise and adoption [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000]. The Ghana residential-building evidence similarly treats sustainability as something to be embedded at every stage of development, but it finds that barriers grouped around management, standards, society, and knowledge hinder implementation, with management-related barriers identified as the most significant obstacle [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Ghana retrofit barrier analysis, sustainability is constrained by cultural, economic, technical knowledge, and regulatory barriers, reinforcing the broader pattern that adoption problems, rather than a lack of sustainability concepts, are the key issue [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. The Saudi “Mostadam” context is not described directly in the supplied evidence, but the other studies suggest that sustainable residential approaches are most effective when they address practical barriers and decision-making across the project lifecycle, rather than relying on awareness alone [https://openalex.org/W4313897987||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386122897||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the studies highlight that environmental sustainability in construction is multi-dimensional, with benefits extending to economic, social, and environmental outcomes, but these gains are limited when regulation, funding, knowledge, and market constraints impede uptake [https://openalex.org/W4321132687||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4221129459||ABSTRACT||000]. The shared sustainability-related finding across the contexts is therefore that identifying barriers and targeting implementation challenges is essential for translating sustainable construction ideas into sustainable residential and broader built-environment outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4283331365||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What did the interviews with retailers and service providers in North America reveal about managing product returns sustainably?
final_answer: Interviews with multichannel retailers, retail experts, and return service providers in the UK and North America found that retailers were mainly focused on the financial impact of returns and had little awareness of the scale of environmental impacts, which meant they lacked a comprehensive approach to managing returns sustainably [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. The same study reported barriers that prevent retailers from developing environmental sustainability plans for returns management, and it proposed strategies and a framework for reducing the environmental impact of returns [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. A related interview-based study suggested that sustainability paradoxes can arise in sustainable practices, including handling product returns, and advised retailers to avoid these paradoxes by shifting toward cradle-to-cradle, closed-loop lifecycle supply chains [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. That study also recommended that retailers evaluate whether the practices they adopt actually support sustainability and consider the full supply chain and each agent’s role in creating sustained competitive advantage [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. Across the evidence, a common theme is that sustainable returns management requires looking beyond immediate financial metrics toward broader lifecycle and supply-chain effects [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, other papers in the set support the importance of circular approaches, such as product recovery in circular supply chains and reuse-oriented distribution systems, while also noting barriers like lack of collaboration, policy support, expertise, technology, and information [https://openalex.org/W4312219350||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4205116137||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What screening criteria and classification rules were used to select and categorize the 87 life cycle assessment studies?
final_answer: The provided evidence does not fully specify a single set of screening criteria and classification rules for the 87 life cycle assessment studies, but it does show several recurring review approaches. One paper says the 87 studies were identified in Scopus for 2017–2023 using the keywords “Sustainability assessment” OR “Life cycle assessment” AND “Internal combustion engine*” OR “ICE*,” followed by careful screening [https://openalex.org/W4393374431||ABSTRACT||001]. That same review then classified the studies across six aspects: sustainability indicators, life cycle phases, life cycle inventories, ICE technologies (including alternative fuels), types of mobile sources, and powertrain systems [https://openalex.org/W4393374431||ABSTRACT||001]. Another paper reports using the PRISMA protocol and a literature search in scientific databases, then applying an evaluation matrix and several integrated criteria to organize studies, although it does not give the exact screening rules [https://openalex.org/W3130637975||ABSTRACT||000]. query: What thematic analysis procedure and inter-coder reliability metrics were used to analyze the interviews, focus groups, and observations?
final_answer: Across the relevant qualitative studies, interviews, focus groups, and observations were analyzed with thematic analysis, but the exact procedures varied. In one multiple-case qualitative study, thematic analysis was carried out during data collection alongside analytical questioning and systemic modeling, and the process was explicitly strengthened through critical reflexive dialogue among the research team, collaborators, and an expert panel [pmc_PMC10136404||ABSTRACT||001]. In another study, the analysis was more elaborately structured: the interviews, focus groups, and observations yielded 727 codes that were organized into 92 sub-themes, then abstracted into 18 themes and one meta-theme, with deductive coding used to group sub-themes across questions into themes related to uncertainty management theory [pmc_PMC9890239||ABSTRACT||002]. A third paper used a deductive/inductive thematic analysis to identify meaningful patterns, but the provided evidence does not indicate that it analyzed interviews, focus groups, or observations [https://openalex.org/W4281686775||ABSTRACT||001]. None of the qualitative papers in the provided evidence reported inter-coder reliability metrics such as agreement percentages, kappa, or similar measures for thematic coding [pmc_PMC10136404||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9890239||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4281686775||ABSTRACT||001]. One unrelated reliability study did report intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), but these were for AIS coding in head injury registry data rather than qualitative interview, focus group, or observation analysis [pmc_PMC10229665||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10229665||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that thematic analysis was used in a reflexive, inductive/deductive, and theme-hierarchizing way across the qualitative studies, but formal inter-coder reliability reporting was absent in the provided summaries [pmc_PMC10136404||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9890239||ABSTRACT||002].
